A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same pFedMoAP research. Their text, equations, tables, and figures support comparison. v1 ends after the references; v3 adds a readable Appendix A.

before.justification: Section 5 reports original experiments across nine datasets, including comparative accuracies in Tables 1–4 and ablations in Figures 3–4.

after.justification: v3 retains those original experiments and adds measured privacy, gating-network, expert-count, feature-dimension, and attention-contribution results in Appendix A.

M1.justification: The core pFedMoAP architecture, objectives, expert selection, and Algorithm 1 remain unchanged. Appendix A.2 adds an evaluated differential-privacy adaptation that clips prompt gradients and adds noise to uploaded prompts, introducing limited training and communication operations.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same five CLIP classification datasets, CIFAR10/100, DomainNet, and Office-Caltech10 with the same label- and feature-shift coverage. The added privacy and architectural studies vary procedures and configurations within these retained tasks and datasets.

E2.justification: The comparator sets in the original benchmark tables remain unchanged. Appendix Table 7 newly evaluates linear-projection gating with three and ten experts and an aggregated attention gate against the proposed local attention gate. The additional related-work citations do not introduce evaluated benchmark baselines.

E3.justification: Appendix A adds privacy experiments with epsilon 25/50 and delta 0.05, gate-aggregation controls, expert-count sweeps on DomainNet and CIFAR10, and pooled feature dimensions from 32 to 1024. Separately, Section 5.1 corrects CIFAR's stated client count from 10 to 100, agreeing with v1's existing caption and discussion; this does not establish rerunning the original experiments.

E4.justification: v1 analyzes shot count and the local-logit coefficient. v3 retains those analyses and adds privacy-noise robustness, attention versus linear gating, local versus aggregated gating, sensitivity to expert count and feature dimension, and attention-contribution visualizations. These substantially expand tests of architectural choices and operating conditions.

E5.justification: Section 5.2 in both versions specifies means and standard deviations over three runs with different seeds. The added tables continue this reporting practice without announcing additional runs, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: The original benchmark values and Figures 3–4 are retained, including the renumbered CIFAR and DomainNet tables. Appendix A adds substantial results: Table 7 reports Flowers102 accuracy of 69.64±4.57 for ten-expert linear gating versus 98.41±0.04 for local attention gating; Table 6 reports 98.36±0.12 for private pFedMoAP at epsilon 25. Further results cover expert count, feature dimension, and attention contributions.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions, objectives, and derivations in Equations 1–11 remain unchanged. The added privacy experiments and citation to a theoretical federated-learning framework introduce no new formal definition, theorem, proof, or mathematical guarantee.

C1.justification: The introduction retains the same three contributions: sharing unaggregated prompts, personalized attention-based prompt mixtures, and empirical superiority across nine datasets. Although the abstract and conclusion are shortened, the central novelty, applicability, and comparative-performance claims remain.

C2.justification: Appendix A adds explanations linking prompt provenance and KNN selection to privacy risk, local gating to noise tolerance, gate aggregation to reduced personalization, additional experts to diminishing returns, and large feature dimensions to overparameterization. It also interprets attention weights as expert contributions and claims every expert is indispensable, an inference stronger than the visualization alone establishes.

D1.justification: Table 5 newly documents dataset training/test sizes and class counts; the appendix supplies configurations, gate sizes, and attention-averaging procedures for its added studies. v3 also provides a repository link and states code availability, replacing v1's promised public release upon acceptance. Existing backbone, optimizer, learning-rate, and epoch details are retained; repository availability was not independently checked.

R1.justification: v3 adds references to Cai et al., Deng et al., FedTP, and Pan et al. in its research context, plus Collins et al. and Dwork for appendix discussions. These modestly broaden coverage of personalization, prompt-learning theory, and privacy while preserving the original positioning around unaggregated prompt sharing.

P1.justification: The abstract and conclusion are condensed, several related-work and evaluation passages are edited, and Appendix A introduces four organized subsections. The main section sequence and most explanatory prose, including the method exposition, remain intact.

P2.justification: v3 adds Tables 5–9, an expert-count curve in Figure 5, and six contribution charts in Figure 6. The original figures remain; the CIFAR and DomainNet tables exchange numbering, DomainNet moves beside Office-Caltech10, and best-score bolding and associated caption statements are removed from the original tables.

improvement.justification: v1's central arguments for attention-based and locally maintained gating lacked direct experimental controls. v3's Table 7 tests both choices, while Tables 8–9 examine dependence on expert count and feature dimension, substantially strengthening validation of the design. Dataset statistics and stated code access also improve reproducibility. Privacy guarantees remain under-specified, and attention weights do not prove expert indispensability, but these limitations do not outweigh the stronger evidence supporting the central architecture.
